## Keep or rush

In class order. Planned total 73 of the 80 minutes.

| Item | Min | | If short |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Discussion 1: the rule each student brought; its two errors; which criterion is behind ProPublica's sentence and behind the replies | 8 | Rush | Question 2 only, with hands: ProPublica's sentence is an error rate (separation), the replies a predictive value (sufficiency) |
| Coding 1: COMPAS from ProPublica's file; the rates at cutoff 5, the sweep, decile 5, a cutoff per group, with feedback | 30 | Keep | Steps 1, 4 and 5; show the sweep plot and the decile-5 table from the complete sheet |
| Problem 1: the fraud checks; why the error rates differ, and a lower bound on the ratio of false positive rates, with feedback | 16 | Keep | (a) to (c), then say (d): if fewer than one UK request in ten would be declined, non-UK requests that should be approved are referred more than twice as often |
| Discussion 2: which criterion, for COMPAS and for the fraud checks; how to decide; the sentence to the losers | 8 | Keep | Question 3 only |
| Discussion 3: the kidney equation; which error, for whom | 10 | Rush; cut first | Question 1 with hands, then question 3 |
| The task for next time | 1 | Keep | Read the task aloud |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,6,14,46]"}

Minimum class, about 55 minutes: coding steps 1, 4 and 5, problem 1
(a) to (c), discussion 2's question 3 and the task for next time. With
more time, add discussion 3 back first, then discussion 1. "Three
views" at the end of the sheet is only for a room that finishes early.

## If you read on

How it runs

- The exercises at the top of the sheet rederive or apply the lecture's
  results; students do them on their own time and the class does not
  work them. Open the
  [complete class sheet](https://ethics4ds.com/teachers/wk07/class_complete.html)
  on screen: green boxes are hints, opened in order after a few minutes;
  blue boxes are answers and example answers.
- The coding reads ProPublica's published file from GitHub, so each
  pair needs a laptop with R, `dplyr`, `ggplot2` and an internet
  connection; it loads in a few seconds. The file has one row per
  defendant with names and dates of birth, which is why the first lines
  keep three columns. If GitHub is blocked for a pair, they work with a
  neighbor. The convention for the week, said once in the lecture: 1 is
  the bad outcome, and flagged and selected mean the same.
- Problem 1 uses an example from the lecture's opening (the DWP's
  model for universal credit advances). The lecture showed the two
  published ratios, 2.27 and 0.97, but not the argument; this is where
  students make it. The argument uses the reported ratios for one year
  and does not depend on the 0.97 being exactly 1.
- Discussion 3 picks up the lecture's kidney example. The point is that
  neither equation is right on average for Black patients, so the
  choice was which error, for whom; the lecture said so but did not
  stop on it.
- Every item ends with a question about who the error falls on, who
  gains from the number reported, or who the choice could be justified
  to. Those questions are the point of the class. A group that has the
  number and skips the question has not finished; ask it.

What students should see

- At cutoff 5: FPR 0.448 and 0.235, FNR 0.280 and 0.477, PPV 0.630 and
  0.591, selected 0.588 and 0.348 (Black and white defendants).
- At decile exactly 5: 48 and 46 percent re-arrested, below either PPV.
- With cutoffs 6 and 4: FPR 0.343 and 0.350, FNR 0.372 and 0.360, PPV
  0.659 and 0.543. Other pairs within two points: (7, 5), (8, 6), (10, 9).
- Fraud checks: correct referrals per request 2.20 times as many;
  incorrect ones more than 2.27 times; with equal PPVs and fewer than
  10 percent of UK requests declined on review, the ratio of FPRs is
  above 2.04.

Where they get stuck

- Conditioning the wrong way: FNR averages over the people who
  reoffended, PPV over the people flagged.
- In step 4, writing two `filter()` calls instead of indexing
  `cutoff[race]`.
- In problem 1, reading the 0.97 as "the model is fair": it is the
  predictive value, and the problem is about what it leaves out.
- Treating "fair by two criteria" as settled; exercise 3 has a rule
  that is wrong about everyone and passes both.
